topic: Why Punjab is stranger than you think: Kartarpur seen from India
hook: Your binoculars can show you a holy shrine in Pakistan, from a field in India.
title: Why Punjab Is Stranger Than You Think
description:
Punjab is split between India and Pakistan, yet from the Indian side people could look across the border at Gurdwara Darbar Sahib in Kartarpur. This video covers the land of five rivers, two scripts for one language, the Grand Trunk Road, the evening ceremony at Attari-Wagah, the 2025 Ravi flood and the Kartarpur Corridor, which was reported shut at the latest reports. Facts were checked against news reports at the time of writing, so check for updates on the corridor's status before you plan a trip.

#Punjab #Kartarpur #IndiaPakistan
comment_prompt: Have you ever seen Kartarpur from the Indian side?

chapters.title: The river that floods a shrine

scenes.narration: Your binoculars can show you a holy shrine in Pakistan, from a field in India.
scenes.headline: Seen From India

scenes.narration: That is not a trick. For years, people really stood on the Indian side and looked across the border at it.
scenes.headline: Really Seen

scenes.narration: By the end of this video, you will see exactly how that works, and why Punjab is stranger than you think.
scenes.headline: Strange Punjab

scenes.narration: Start with the name. Punjab is a maths problem hiding in plain sight.
scenes.headline: Name Is Maths

scenes.narration: Panj means five and ab means water in Persian, so Punjab means the land of five waters.
scenes.headline: Five Waters

scenes.narration: Those five rivers are the Jhelum, the Chenab, the Ravi, the Beas and the Sutlej.
scenes.headline: The Five Rivers

scenes.narration: Before 1947, all five flowed through one Punjab. After 1947, that one land became two, in two countries.
scenes.headline: One Land, Two

scenes.narration: Indian Punjab and Pakistani Punjab share a name, a history, and the same way of speaking, but not a flag.
scenes.headline: Same Name, Two Flags

scenes.narration: Walk across a Punjab field and the soil looks exactly the same on both sides, even though the countries are different.
scenes.headline: Same Soil

scenes.narration: Now here is the first twist. A language you can hear on both sides, but cannot read on the other.
scenes.headline: Hear It, Can't Read It

scenes.narration: In Indian Punjab, Punjabi is written in Gurmukhi, the script of Sikh scripture, which runs left to right.
scenes.headline: Gurmukhi Script

scenes.narration: In Pakistani Punjab, the same language is written in Shahmukhi, which looks like Urdu and runs right to left.
scenes.headline: Shahmukhi Script

scenes.narration: So two friends can speak the same sentence, laugh at the same joke, and still not read each other's signboards.
scenes.headline: Same Joke, Two Signs

scenes.narration: Punjabi is actually the most spoken mother tongue in Pakistan. Same songs, same proverbs, two alphabets, one line on a map.
scenes.headline: Two Alphabets

scenes.narration: Stay with me, because the next one is a road older than most countries, and a border cuts it in half.
scenes.headline: A Road Cut Open

scenes.narration: It is the Grand Trunk Road, one of the oldest and longest roads in South Asia.
scenes.headline: Grand Trunk Road

scenes.narration: For centuries it carried traders, armies and pilgrims, from Bengal in the east all the way to Kabul.
scenes.headline: Bengal To Kabul

scenes.narration: Ordinary families used it too, with bullock carts and bags of grain, long before anyone drew a border on it.
scenes.headline: Before Any Border

scenes.narration: It passes through Amritsar in India. Cross the border, and the same road reaches Lahore in Pakistan.
scenes.headline: Amritsar To Lahore

scenes.narration: Two of Punjab's great cities sit on one ancient road, but today you cannot just drive from one to the other.
scenes.headline: No Simple Drive

scenes.narration: The road meets the border at Attari on the Indian side, and Wagah on the Pakistani side.
scenes.headline: Attari And Wagah

scenes.narration: And right there, where the road ends in a gate, there is a show every single evening.
scenes.headline: A Show At A Gate

scenes.narration: Every evening, soldiers from two armies perform a ceremony for huge crowds. It is called Beating Retreat.
scenes.headline: Beating Retreat

scenes.narration: Border Security Force men stand on the Indian side. Pakistan Rangers stand on the other.
scenes.headline: Two Armies, One Show

scenes.narration: They march in heavy boots, wear tall fan-shaped headgear, and kick their legs up as high as they can.
scenes.headline: Legs Up High

scenes.narration: The crowds on both sides cheer, and each side tries to be louder than the other.
scenes.headline: Loudest Crowd Wins

scenes.narration: Then both flags are lowered at the same time, folded, and the gates are shut.
scenes.headline: Flags Come Down

scenes.narration: It is part theatre, part serious military routine, and it has run for decades at a border most people never see.
scenes.headline: Decades Of Ritual

scenes.narration: But the strangest part is not the show. It is what lies a few kilometres away from another gate on this border.
scenes.headline: Another Gate

scenes.narration: That gate matters far more to millions of people. It leads to a guru's home, and first, we need the river.
scenes.headline: A Guru's Gate

scenes.narration: The Ravi is one of those five waters, and in 2025 it did something dramatic.
scenes.headline: The Ravi Rises

scenes.narration: Heavy monsoon rain swelled the Ravi until it overflowed, in late August 2025.
scenes.headline: Monsoon Flood

scenes.narration: News reports said the whole Kartarpur complex, including Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, went under floodwater.
scenes.headline: Shrine Under Water

scenes.narration: Reports said around 150 people were rescued, and the Guru Granth Sahib was moved to the first floor, above the water.
scenes.headline: 150 Rescued

scenes.narration: A border cannot stop a river. The Ravi does not check passports. It simply flows from India into Pakistan.
scenes.headline: River Needs No Visa

scenes.narration: That is the lesson of Punjab. The land was split. The water was not.
scenes.headline: Land Split, Water Not

scenes.narration: If you like strange places and facts like this, subscribe, because there is more like it every day.
scenes.headline: Subscribe

scenes.narration: Now the shrine I promised you. Its name is Gurdwara Darbar Sahib, in a town called Kartarpur.
scenes.headline: Darbar Sahib

scenes.narration: Kartarpur is where Guru Nanak, the founder of Sikhism, settled in his later years, beside the Ravi.
scenes.headline: Guru Nanak's Home

scenes.narration: He did not live in a palace. He farmed the land there, and shared meals with everyone who came.
scenes.headline: A Farming Guru

scenes.narration: He died at Kartarpur in 1539, and that is where this story gets even stranger.
scenes.headline: Died In 1539

scenes.narration: The story says Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs all claimed him, and each wanted to honour him in their own way.
scenes.headline: Three Faiths Claim Him

scenes.narration: They were told to place flowers beside him. By morning, the story goes, only the cloth and the flowers remained.
scenes.headline: Only Flowers Remained

scenes.narration: So the gurdwara today holds both a samadhi and a grave, side by side, for one man loved by many faiths.
scenes.headline: Samadhi And Grave

scenes.narration: Then 1947 arrived, and the new border left Kartarpur in Pakistan, just across the river from India.
scenes.headline: Left Across The Line

scenes.narration: Ask older families in Punjab about 1947, and many describe a home or a shrine that suddenly lay in another country.
scenes.headline: Home In Another Country

scenes.narration: For Sikhs in India, their holiest places in Pakistan suddenly became places they could only pray towards.
scenes.headline: Prayed Towards It

scenes.narration: In their daily prayer, Sikhs have asked for open access to the gurdwaras that were left behind in Pakistan.
scenes.headline: A Daily Prayer

scenes.narration: The nearest Indian town is Dera Baba Nanak, in Gurdaspur district, only a few kilometres from the border.
scenes.headline: Dera Baba Nanak

scenes.narration: There, a raised viewing platform was opened in 2008, with binoculars put there by the Border Security Force.
scenes.headline: The Viewing Platform

scenes.narration: Pilgrims climbed up, raised the binoculars, and looked across the fields towards a distant white building.
scenes.headline: Look Across The Fields

scenes.narration: Some wept. Some folded their hands. Some simply stood there, because they could not go any closer.
scenes.headline: Hands Folded

scenes.narration: On foggy days, reports said, the view was hard, but people still came, just to face the right direction.
scenes.headline: Fog On The Fields

scenes.narration: Distance was never the problem. The shrine is only about four or five kilometres away from the Indian border.
scenes.headline: Only A Few Km

scenes.narration: The problem was that a fence stood between a person and a place their family had prayed towards for generations.
scenes.headline: A Fence Between

scenes.narration: Then, in November 2019, something rare happened. The two governments opened a corridor.
scenes.headline: The Corridor Opens

scenes.narration: It opened around the 550th birth anniversary of Guru Nanak, and it was built for one purpose.
scenes.headline: 550th Anniversary

scenes.narration: Indian pilgrims could go from Dera Baba Nanak straight to Kartarpur, with a permit, but without a visa.
scenes.headline: Walk Without A Visa

scenes.narration: Think about that. A pilgrim could go in the morning, pray at the very place of Guru Nanak, and be back by evening.
scenes.headline: Back By Evening

scenes.narration: For the first time in decades, thousands could see the shrine not through glass lenses, but with their own eyes.
scenes.headline: Not Through Lenses

scenes.narration: Two countries that rarely agree on anything agreed to keep this one path open for faith.
scenes.headline: A Rare Agreement

scenes.narration: The corridor agreement was even extended, and it now runs until October 2029.
scenes.headline: Deal Till 2029

scenes.narration: But the path has not stayed open. In May 2025, India suspended the corridor amid rising tensions.
scenes.headline: Corridor Suspended

scenes.narration: At the latest reports I could find, it was still shut, with no date given for it to reopen.
scenes.headline: Still Shut

scenes.narration: So the old way is the way people fall back on. Stand on the Indian side, and look across the fields.
scenes.headline: Back To Binoculars

scenes.narration: Look at what that means. A holy place that was once a short walk is again a distant white shape on the horizon.
scenes.headline: A White Shape

scenes.narration: Both sides look at the same sky, and the same Ravi river runs between them, as if nothing had changed.
scenes.headline: Same Sky, Same River

scenes.narration: And behind that one shape, there are five rivers, two alphabets, one ancient road, and one ceremony of marching soldiers.
scenes.headline: It All Connects

scenes.narration: Punjab is a place where the map says two things, and the people feel one.
scenes.headline: Map Versus Heart

scenes.narration: So the next time someone tells you geography is boring, ask them about the shrine you can see from India.
scenes.headline: Geography Isn't Boring

scenes.narration: Your binoculars really can show you a holy shrine in Pakistan, from a field in India, and now you know why.
scenes.headline: The Loop

scenes.narration: Next in this series: another place that sounds fake, but is completely real. See you there.
scenes.headline: Next Time
